paragraphs: Management of hypertension, alone or with other antihypertensives. This reference concerns standalone bisoprolol fumarate tablets; bisoprolol/hydrochlorothiazide combinations have another active ingredient and different dose/product considerations. No pediatric indication is established.

The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline recommends bisoprolol as one of three evidence-based beta blockers for HFrEF with current/prior symptoms, reducing mortality/hospitalization. This is distinct from the selected U.S. hypertension indication and from starting treatment in overt unstable failure.

Usual hypertension start: 5 mg once daily; selected patients may start 2.5 mg. If inadequate, increase to 10 mg then 20 mg daily as needed. CrCl < 40 mL/min or hepatic impairment (hepatitis/cirrhosis): start 2.5 mg daily and titrate cautiously. No age-only reduction is required unless significant renal/hepatic dysfunction. Limited data suggest it is not dialyzable; routine dialysis replacement is unnecessary.

paragraphs: Guideline table: 1.25 mg once daily initially, target 10 mg daily as tolerated; GDMT reassessment/titration can occur every 1–2 weeks depending on symptoms, vital signs and labs. These are HFrEF guidance, not the 20 mg hypertension ceiling. Selected current U.S. tablets are 5/10 mg; the prescriber/pharmacist must establish an appropriate validated low-dose formulation, rather than assume a quarter-tablet or home-compounded dose is accurate.

Take the prescribed oral dose once daily; food does not affect absorption. In bronchospastic disease, generally avoid beta blockers; if necessary after other antihypertensive intolerance/failure, the label starts 2.5 mg with the lowest effective dose and available beta-2 bronchodilator. Do not interrupt independently. The label advises tapering over approximately one week under observation, including patients without evident coronary disease; withdrawal symptoms may require temporary reinstitution. Obtain missed-dose instructions and do not independently double.

Beta blockade can worsen contractility or precipitate failure; evaluate new/worsening dyspnea, edema, poor perfusion or excessive bradycardia. Abrupt withdrawal can worsen angina or cause MI/ventricular arrhythmia. Peripheral arterial symptoms may worsen. Bronchospasm remains possible, especially as selectivity falls at higher doses. Hypoglycemia signs, particularly tachycardia, and thyrotoxicosis can be masked; sudden withdrawal may precipitate thyroid storm. Do not routinely withdraw chronic therapy before major surgery, but tell the anesthesia team. Severe-allergy history may increase reactivity and reduce response to usual epinephrine doses.

Selected label: cardiogenic shock, overt cardiac failure, second- or third-degree AV block and marked sinus bradycardia. Do not silently add a pacemaker exception absent from this label or erase the overt-failure restriction because of chronic HFrEF guideline use. Bronchospastic disease is a strong avoidance/caution warning rather than a listed formal contraindication.
The selected current Micro Labs label has no boxed warning. Its abrupt-discontinuation warning remains clinically important; absence of a box does not permit unsupervised stopping.

Fatigue/asthenia, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, bradycardia and hypotension are reported; bronchospasm, worsening failure and severe allergy are important less-common risks. Trial-listed experiences do not establish drug causality for every event. Sporadic liver-test and other lab abnormalities are described. Overdose can cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, failure, bronchospasm and hypoglycemia: seek emergency/poison-center assessment; hospital supportive treatment may be required and dialysis is not expected to clear it effectively.
Medication reconciliation includes ophthalmic and other beta blockers.

paragraphs: No clinically relevant PK interaction was documented with studied thiazides/cimetidine, and no prothrombin-time effect was seen with stable warfarin. These observations do not remove additive antihypertensive effects, co-drug risks or the need for patient-specific review.

CrCl < 40 mL/min prolongs half-life about threefold; cirrhosis slows/varies elimination. Start 2.5 mg daily in labeled renal/hepatic impairment and titrate cautiously. Older adults need no age-only dose change, but renal function and pulse/BP may limit tolerance. No pediatric safety/effectiveness or dose is established.

No adequate controlled pregnancy studies; animal fetal toxicity at high exposures supports individualized benefit/risk assessment. Use in pregnancy only when potential benefit justifies fetal risk. Human milk excretion is unknown in the selected label; small amounts entered rat milk, so exercise caution and assess infant/maternal needs rather than claim established lactation safety.

Bisoprolol has no significant intrinsic sympathomimetic or membrane-stabilizing activity at therapeutic doses. Antihypertensive effects may involve lower cardiac output, reduced renin and reduced central sympathetic outflow. It slows sinus/AV-node function; at doses ≥ 20 mg it also blocks beta-2 receptors. BP/pulse effects can persist 24 hours.

Oral bioavailability about 80%; peak 2–4 hours, protein binding about 30%, half-life 9–12 hours and steady state within 5 days. Roughly half the dose appears unchanged in urine and the remainder mainly as inactive metabolites; renal and nonrenal clearance contribute. Food does not alter absorption. It is not metabolized by CYP2D6; do not infer absence of every other metabolic interaction.

Assess BP/pulse and symptoms before/after initiation and changes. Review dizziness/syncope, excessive bradycardia, chest pain, breathlessness, edema/weight change, peripheral circulation and bronchospasm. Monitor renal/hepatic context for dosing and glucose in at-risk patients. Consider ECG when conduction disease/symptoms or interacting medicines warrant; the label does not require routine serum drug levels.

Take consistently and do not stop/taper without a plan. Report slow-pulse symptoms, fainting, new swelling or breathing problems; urgent chest pain needs emergency evaluation. Know effects before driving/operating machinery. Tell clinicians about surgery, asthma, diabetes, thyroid disease and severe allergy. Keep the exact low-dose formulation plan clear when treated for HFrEF; do not substitute a combination tablet.

Micro Labs 5 mg tablet: pink, round, film-coated, deep score on one side and a bar-like imprint on the other; 30-tablet child-resistant bottle NDC 42571-470-30. Verify the actual written label and imprint, not color alone.

Selected standalone oral tablets: 5 and 10 mg; current FDA ANDA218303 lists both Prescription. This profile does not establish U.S. 1.25/2.5 mg tablet stock or any injectable/extended-release standalone product. Hydrochlorothiazide combination strengths/regimens are excluded.

Store 20–25°C, protect from moisture and dispense in tight light-resistant containers. Follow package expiry and child-resistant closure instructions. Dose splitting/compounding for a prescribed low dose requires pharmacist verification; do not infer accurate quartering from a single tablet score.

fields.name: Bisoprolol
fields.description: An oral beta-1-selective blocker labeled for hypertension. Guideline-supported chronic HFrEF use is distinguished from the U.S. product indication, with lower starting doses, tolerance assessment and a verified formulation plan.
facts: Standalone oral tablets · hypertension and distinct HFrEF guidance

essential.title: Check pulse, conduction and heart-failure stability before dosing.
essential.text: Marked bradycardia, advanced AV block, shock and overt cardiac failure are label contraindications. Chronic stable HFrEF use requires a separate supervised plan. Do not stop abruptly; coronary events can follow withdrawal. Beta-1 selectivity does not eliminate bronchospasm or masked hypoglycemia.
